area: Area V. Performance and Ground Reference Maneuvers
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how a steep spiral sheds altitude while staying over one spot, how wind changes the bank you need, and how to protect the engine and the airframe, and fly at least three 360° gliding turns around a point within commercial standards (bank no more than 60°, airspeed ±10 knots, rollout ±10°, finished no lower than 1,500 feet AGL).
why: The steep spiral is a way to get rid of a lot of altitude quickly while staying over a chosen spot, which is exactly what you want when the engine quits high above a good field [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. It also trains wind correction, airspeed control in a glide and division of attention, all with the ground turning under a steeply banked wing [[24:213|AFH 10-4]] [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

prereading.label: AFH 7-2 to 7-4

prereading.label: AFH 7-7 to 7-8

prereading.what: Emergency descent in general, glides, best glide speed, and gliding turns (why they need more back pressure and less rudder).
prereading.label: AFH 3-21 to 3-24

prereading.what: Simulated emergency landings: spiraling down over the field to the key position, and keeping the engine warm and cleared.
prereading.label: AFH 9-28 to 9-29

warmup: Think first: your engine quits 5,000 feet above a long, smooth hay field. Gliding straight ahead would carry you miles past it. How could you get down to pattern altitude without ever losing sight of that field, and what would the wind do to your circle while you tried?

key_terms.def: A gliding turn of constant radius around a point on the ground, flown as at least three 360° turns, to lose a lot of altitude while staying over one spot [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].
A prominent object on the ground, easy to see yet small enough to be precise, that you circle at a constant distance [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].
Your speed over the ground. Headed downwind it is higher than your airspeed; headed upwind it is lower [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].
The sideways movement of the airplane over the ground caused by the moving air mass [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
The angle you point the nose into the wind to cancel drift and hold a ground track [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
The airspeed that gives the greatest forward distance for a given loss of altitude in still air, at maximum lift-to-drag ratio [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].
A maneuver to descend as rapidly as possible to a lower altitude or to the ground, without exceeding structural limits [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
Advancing the throttle for a few seconds during a long idle glide to keep the engine warm and avoid plug fouling and carburetor ice [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
Abrupt engine temperature change caused by the extra cooling air of a high-speed descent [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]].
A nose-low upset: a descending turn in which airspeed and G-load can increase rapidly [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].
In a long coordinated turn you sense wings level while descending, pull back, and only tighten the spiral and lose more altitude [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].
The red line on the airspeed indicator, the limit beyond which structural damage could occur [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]].

chunks.title: The steep spiral at commercial standards

body.p: A steep spiral is a gliding turn in which you keep a constant radius around a point on the ground. It looks like turns around a point, except the airplane is descending fast. You fly at least three 360° turns, and you start high enough to finish no lower than 1,500 feet AGL [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

head: What the examiner checks
Commercial ACS standard
rows: Select an altitude sufficient to continue through a series of at least three, 360° turns (ACS CA.V.B.S2)
Establish and maintain a steep spiral, not to exceed 60° angle of bank, to maintain a constant radius about a suitable ground reference point (ACS CA.V.B.S3)
Apply wind-drift correction to track a constant radius circle around selected reference point with bank not to exceed 60° a steepest point in turn (ACS CA.V.B.S4)
Divide attention between airplane control, traffic avoidance and the ground track while maintaining coordinated flight (ACS CA.V.B.S5)
Specified airspeed ±10 knots; roll out toward an object or specified heading ±10°; complete the maneuver no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS CA.V.B.S6)

callout.text: For an initial commercial ASEL applicant, the examiner must pick Steep Turns or Steep Spiral (ACS Appendix 3, Area V). You will not know which one until the flight, so prepare both.

There is no altitude tolerance in the usual sense. The hard floor is 1,500 feet AGL at the end of the maneuver (ACS CA.V.B.S6). Running out of altitude before the third turn is a failure of planning (ACS CA.V.B.S2).

check.q: What three numbers set the commercial tolerances for the steep spiral?
check.a: Airspeed ±10 knots, rollout ±10°, and finish no lower than 1,500 feet AGL; the bank must never exceed 60° (ACS CA.V.B.S3, S6).

chunks.title: Why it matters: getting down over a field

body.p: The AFH gives the steep spiral one purpose: to lose a lot of altitude quickly while staying over a selected spot. It may be useful during an emergency landing [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

Picture an engine failure high above a good field. In a simulated emergency landing you may use any mix of gliding maneuvers, from wings level to spirals, to arrive at the normal key position at normal traffic pattern altitude. From the key point on, it is a normal power-off approach [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

bullets: Hold a constant gliding speed. Changing speeds ruins your judgment of glide distance and the landing spot [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
Note how much altitude each turn costs. In a real emergency that tells you when to roll out so you are neither too high nor too low [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
Practice rolling out on a heading into the wind or at right angles to it, not just toward an object. That is the skill you would use for a real approach [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
With lots of altitude, inexperienced pilots tend to delay choosing a field and misjudge the glide [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

callout.text: Eagerness to get down is a classic fault. You cannot dive at a field and expect to land on it; too much speed causes floating and overshooting [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].
Application: on your first practice turn, read the altimeter at the same point each lap. That number per lap is your planning tool for the rest of the spiral.

check.q: In an engine-out spiral over a field, where do you want the spiral to end?
check.a: At the normal key position at normal traffic pattern altitude, then fly a normal power-off approach [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

body.p: The two maneuvers look alike because both lose altitude fast in a turn. The AFH warns that the reasons for them may differ and that the airspeed and configuration are usually different [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

head: Steep spiral
Emergency descent
rows: Lose altitude while staying over a selected spot [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]
Descend as soon and as fast as possible, for example for fire or loss of pressurization [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]
Idle, carburetor heat on if equipped [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]
Idle unless the manufacturer prohibits it [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]
High: the maximum allowed for the procedure, not past VNE, VLE or VFE [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]
Not set by the AFH for this maneuver; follow the POH and your CFI
High drag: gear and flaps as the manufacturer recommends [[24:82|AFH 3-21]] [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]
Up to 60°, varied for wind (ACS CA.V.B.S3, S4)
About 30° to 45° to keep positive G [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]

body.p: So a steep spiral is a slow, controlled, ground-referenced glide. An emergency descent is a fast, high-drag dive whose job is speed of descent, with a turn to look for traffic below and a landing spot [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

callout.text: Some airplanes have a specific emergency descent procedure in the AFM/POH. Use it [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

check.q: Name two ways the steep spiral differs from an emergency descent.
check.a: Lower airspeed (gliding speed versus maximum allowed speed) and a different purpose and configuration: staying over a spot versus descending as fast as possible with high drag [[24:212|AFH 10-3]] [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

chunks.title: Wind, groundspeed and the ground track

body.p: The airplane flies in a moving body of air. Like a boat in a current, it is carried along with the air, so its path over the ground is not the path it flies through the air [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

Headed upwind, your groundspeed is lower than your airspeed. Headed downwind, it is higher [[24:149|AFH 7-3]]. Hold one bank angle all the way around and the circle over the ground stretches: the radius grows as groundspeed grows and shrinks as groundspeed falls [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].

The AFH demonstration: fly a constant medium-bank 360° over a straight road. In the air the circle is perfect, but over the ground it is not, and you end up downwind of where you started [[24:150|AFH 7-4]].

bullets: Wind affects groundspeed most when it is parallel to your heading, and least when it is at right angles to it [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].
Pilots do not calculate drift corrections in ground reference maneuvers. They use the references and adjust to cancel drift [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].
Learn to read the wind from smoke, dust, water and windsocks; you will need it for an emergency field too [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

callout.text: In a steep spiral you descend through the air layers, so the wind can change on the way down. Keep correcting for changes in wind direction and speed all the way [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

check.q: At a constant bank, what happens to your circle over the ground as you turn from upwind to downwind?
check.a: Groundspeed increases, so the radius over the ground increases and you drift outward [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].

body.p: To keep a constant radius over the ground you change the bank as groundspeed changes: steeper bank when groundspeed is higher, shallower when it is lower [[24:149|AFH 7-3]]. The AFH steep spiral says it plainly: steepen the bank on downwind headings and shallow it on upwind headings [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

Why it works: at a higher groundspeed you have less time to get around the circle, so you need a faster rate of turn, and that takes more bank. At a lower groundspeed you have more time, so less bank [[24:150|AFH 7-4]].

AFH worked example: downwind at 100 knots groundspeed in a 45° bank gives a radius over the ground of about 890 feet. At the upwind point, groundspeed is lower and about 33° holds the same radius [[24:150|AFH 7-4]]. You can check it with the PHAK radius formula, radius = speed squared / (11.26 x tan bank), using groundspeed: 100 x 100 / 11.26 = 888 feet [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].

bullets: Downwind half of the circle: the nose points progressively toward the inside of the turn, so the heading is ahead of your position [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].
Upwind half: the nose points progressively toward the outside, so the heading is behind your position [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].
Your distance from the reference sets the radius. Pick it so the steepest bank, headed downwind, stays at or below 60° [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

callout.text: Fast over the ground, steep. Slow over the ground, shallow. Downwind steep, upwind shallow.
The 60° limit is at the steepest point (ACS CA.V.B.S4). If you would need more than 60° downwind, the circle is too tight for the wind; widen it.

check.q: Where in the circle is the bank steepest, and why?
check.a: Headed downwind, because groundspeed is highest there and you need the fastest rate of turn to hold the radius [[24:212|AFH 10-3]] [[24:150|AFH 7-4]].

chunks.title: Airspeed control in a gliding turn

body.p: Holding a constant airspeed is a core skill here, because the airspeed tends to wander every time the bank changes. Expect it, and make your pitch corrections ahead of the bank changes [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

Three things push the nose down and raise the speed in a gliding turn: less vertical lift because the lift is tilted, too much rudder because control pressures feel light, and the airplane's natural nose-down tendency with power off. So a gliding turn needs more back pressure than a straight glide or a level turn [[24:84|AFH 3-23]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

bullets: Steepening the bank downwind: add back pressure as you roll in, or the nose drops and speed builds (application of [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]).
Shallowing the bank upwind: ease the back pressure, or the nose rises and speed falls. The AFH warns the same when recovering from a gliding turn to a straight glide [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].
Use sound, sight and control feel together. Rising wind noise means rising speed [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Do not chase the airspeed indicator; set the attitude on the horizon, then cross-check [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

body.p: Coordination feels different without power. The design corrections for P-factor and slipstream stay in while those effects disappear, so slight left rudder is likely needed in a glide [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Rudder pressures are lighter, and pilots used to powered flight often push too much and slip or skid [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

callout.text: Trim for the gliding speed before you roll in, then let the bank changes be the only thing you fly. The ACS standard is the specified airspeed ±10 knots (ACS CA.V.B.S6).

check.q: You roll steeper headed downwind and do nothing else. What happens to airspeed?
check.a: It increases: the tilted lift and the nose-down tendency drop the nose unless you add back pressure [[24:85|AFH 3-24]] [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

chunks.title: Load factor, stall speed and the 60° limit

body.p: Bank costs load. In a level coordinated turn, 45° gives 1.41 G and 60° gives 2.0 G, in any airplane at any airspeed [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor: an airplane that stalls at 50 knots stalls at 70 knots in a level 60° turn [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

The PHAK lists stalling by raising the load factor 'as in a steep turn or spiral' as a danger to know [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. Application: a steep spiral is flown at gliding speed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]], which is not far above the stall to begin with, so at 60° the margin can shrink to almost nothing.

callout.text: Before ground reference maneuvers the AFH has you find the predicted stall speed at the highest bank you expect, so you know you have a margin [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Do it for 60° before a steep spiral, and compare it with your gliding speed.

body.p: Application: the 1 / cos(bank) figures are for a level turn. In a steady spiral at constant airspeed the numbers are close, but any extra pull while steeply banked adds G and raises the stall speed further.

callout.text: With a passenger who is not a crewmember and no approved parachutes, no intentional maneuver may exceed 60° of bank or 30° nose up or nose down. Flight tests and required maneuvers given by a CFI are excepted [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]].
A low-level gliding steep turn with too much rudder toward the bank and back pressure to save altitude can become an unrecoverable spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

check.q: In a level 60° bank, by about what factor does the stall speed rise?
check.a: About 1.41, the square root of the 2.0 load factor [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

chunks.title: Airspeed limits and the spiral dive

body.p: A steep spiral that loses its airspeed control turns into a different thing: a spiral dive. That is a nose-low upset, a descending turn in which airspeed and G-load can rise fast, often from a botched turn [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. The AFH also names high-speed steep spirals after botched steep turns as a way to reach a sink rate you cannot recover from near the ground [[24:103|AFH 4-17]].

head: Airspeed indicator marking
Meaning
rows: VNE: beyond it structural damage could occur [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]]
VNO to VNE: smooth air only, and then only with caution [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]]
Normal operating range, VS1 to VNO [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]]
Flap operating range, VS0 to VFE [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]]

body.p: Spiral dive recovery, in order [[24:131|AFH 5-26]] [[24:132|AFH 5-27]]:

bullets: 1. Reduce power to idle (in a steep spiral it already is).
2. Apply some forward elevator to unload to about +1 G.
3. Roll wings level with coordinated aileron and rudder.
4. Gently raise the nose to level flight; you may be near or past VNE, so go easy.
5. Once the airspeed has settled at VY, add climb power and climb back to a safe altitude.

callout.text: The startled pilot pulls hard and rolls level at the same time. That rolling pullout can overload the airframe [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Common errors include pulling without rolling level and not unloading first [[24:132|AFH 5-27]].
In turbulence, respect VA as well [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. VA protects only one full control input, one time, in one axis, in smooth air [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

check.q: In a spiral dive, what comes between reducing power and rolling the wings level?
check.a: Some forward elevator to unload the wing to about 1 G [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

chunks.title: Keeping the engine alive: clearing and carburetor ice

body.p: A steep spiral means a long time at idle. That can over-cool the engine, foul the spark plugs or build carburetor ice. So advance the throttle now and then and hold it for a few seconds. Watch the cylinder head temperature gauge if you have one [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

bullets: When you advance the throttle, adjust pitch so the airspeed stays constant [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
Do it preferably while headed into the wind [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Application: that is where groundspeed is lowest, so a brief speed or track change costs the least distance from the circle.
If carburetor ice is possible and you plan closed-throttle operation, put carburetor heat full on before closing the throttle and leave it on [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].
Carburetor heat alone may not be enough; open the throttle smoothly for a few seconds now and then to keep the engine warm [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].
High-speed descents can shock cool the engine with abrupt temperature changes [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]].

body.p: Carburetor ice is most likely below about 70°F with relative humidity above 80 percent, but it can form at temperatures up to 100°F and humidity as low as 50 percent [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]]. It is especially dangerous at reduced power in a descent, because it can build unnoticed until you add power [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

callout.text: This is the emergency landing link again: a spiral that ends with an engine that will not take power is a forced landing. During simulated emergencies, keep the engine warm and cleared, and agree who controls the throttle [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

check.q: When is the best time in the circle to clear the engine, and what do you do with pitch?
check.a: Preferably headed into the wind, adjusting pitch to hold a constant airspeed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

chunks.title: Clearing the area and collision hazards

body.p: Start every steep spiral by clearing the airspace for traffic and hazards [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. A spiral is special because you will descend thousands of feet through other people's altitudes, and the steeply lowered wing blocks part of your view.

bullets: Make clearing turns, two 90° turns looking left, right, above and below [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
Look hardest below. The AFH has simulated emergency descents flown in a turn to check for traffic below [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
Make any radio announcements, such as on a practice area frequency, before you start [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
Scan in steps of no more than 10°, at least 1 second each [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
A target with no relative motion that grows larger is on a collision course [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Move your head to see around door posts and wings; at times lift a wing to look [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

body.p: Pick the reference and the area with care. Stay away from congested areas, open air assemblies and livestock [[24:148|AFH 7-2]], and remember that traffic clusters near VORs, airways and airport surface areas [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

callout.text: 'Not scanning for other traffic during the maneuver' is on the AFH list of steep spiral errors [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Clear before, and keep clearing through every lap.

check.q: Why does a steep spiral call for extra attention below you?
check.a: You descend rapidly through lower altitudes; the AFH has emergency descents flown in a turn to check for traffic below [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

body.p: In one lap you hold airspeed with pitch, change bank for the wind, track the circle, watch for traffic, clear the engine and count altitude. Becoming disoriented and flying by the instruments instead of outside references are both listed steep spiral errors [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

Your eyes are your main orientation source in VMC and usually overrule false sensations [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]]. Keep them outside on the reference, the horizon and the traffic, with quick cross-checks inside.

bullets: Graveyard spiral: in a long coordinated turn you can feel level while losing altitude; pulling back only tightens the spiral [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]] [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].
Coriolis illusion: an abrupt head movement in a prolonged constant-rate turn can create a sense of rotation on another axis. Avoid sudden, extreme head movements [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].
If you drop something, get it with minimal head movement and watch for the Coriolis illusion [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].
In a high-wing airplane the lowered wing may hide the reference, especially in a left turn from the left seat. Change the radius or altitude so the point stays in view [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].

callout.text: Application: count laps out loud ('one', 'two', 'three') at the same point each time and say the altitude. It keeps you oriented and tells you when to plan the rollout.

check.q: Why is the steep spiral a set-up for the graveyard spiral illusion, and what saves you?
check.a: It is a long coordinated turn in which you lose altitude, the exact condition for the illusion [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]; good outside references keep the eyes in charge [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]].

chunks.title: Low altitude: stall, spin and CFIT

body.p: The commercial ACS floor is 1,500 feet AGL at the end of the maneuver, and the AFH says the same (ACS CA.V.B.S6) [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. Plan backward from that floor: three turns at your altitude loss per turn, plus a margin.

bullets: Gliding steep turns near the ground are a known spin trap: too much rudder plus back pressure to hold altitude can become an unrecoverable spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].
Cross-controlling during gliding turns near the ground is a listed error [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].
Unrecoverable sink rates near the ground can happen without a stall, for example a high-speed steep spiral [[24:103|AFH 4-17]].
Anywhere, you must stay high enough for an emergency landing without undue hazard to people or property if the engine fails [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]].

callout.text: In a real engine failure the spiral ends at the key position, not at 1,500 feet [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. Practice is different: in training, terminate before you get low, and never continue a simulated emergency to where it creates an undue hazard [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].
Application: before you roll in, say three numbers: field elevation, the 1,500 AGL floor in MSL, and your start altitude in MSL.

check.q: You lose 450 feet per turn. What is the lowest AGL altitude to start three turns and still meet the ACS?
check.a: 1,500 + 3 x 450 = 2,850 feet AGL, plus a margin (ACS CA.V.B.S2, S6).

body.p: A generic flow from the AFH. Your POH gives the gliding speed, carburetor heat use and any engine limits.

bullets: 1. Find the wind and choose a small, prominent reference point in an area with landing options [[24:154|AFH 7-8]] [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
2. Pick an altitude that finishes three turns no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS CA.V.B.S2, S6).
3. Clear the area, above and especially below [[24:213|AFH 10-4]] [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
4. Close the throttle to idle, carburetor heat on if equipped, and slow to gliding speed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
5. At gliding speed, lower the pitch and roll to the bank you need as the reference point is reached [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
6. Hold a constant radius: steepen downwind, shallow upwind, never past 60° [[24:212|AFH 10-3]] [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
7. Anticipate pitch changes with each bank change to hold airspeed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
8. Clear the engine now and then, preferably into the wind, holding airspeed with pitch [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
9. Note the altitude lost each turn [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
10. After at least three turns, roll out toward the object or heading to a wings-level glide with no change in airspeed, then recover to cruise [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

callout.text: Clear, idle, heat, glide speed, roll in at the point, steep downwind, shallow upwind, clear the engine, count the laps, roll out level at the same speed.

The examiner may ask for a rollout on a heading at right angles to the wind or directly into it instead of toward an object. That is the AFH's harder version, and the one that matters in a real emergency [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

check.q: What should the airplane be doing at the moment the rollout is complete?
check.a: A wings-level glide with no change in airspeed, on the object or heading; then you recover to cruise [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

head: AFH common error
What it looks like
Fix
rows: Rolling in from cruise with no look below
Clearing turns, scan below, radio call [[24:148|AFH 7-2]] [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]
Inadequate pitch control on entry or rollout
Speed jumps as you roll in, or balloons and decays on rollout
Reach gliding speed before lowering the nose; ease back pressure as the bank comes off [[24:213|AFH 10-4]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Lighter rudder in the glide; slight left rudder is normal [[24:84|AFH 3-23]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Trim for gliding speed before roll-in (application)
Anticipate pitch with each bank change [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]
Lost count of laps, lost the point
Eyes outside on the reference and horizon [[24:213|AFH 10-4]] [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]]
Not finishing on the heading or reference
Plan the last lap and start the rollout early enough (ACS CA.V.B.S6)

body.p: Table source: the steep spiral common error list [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]; fixes as cited.

The big one: the nose drops in a steep downwind bank, the speed runs up and the pilot pulls. That is how a steep spiral becomes a spiral dive. Unload, roll level, then raise the nose gently [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

callout.text: Excessive rudder pressure during recovery from gliding turns is a listed error too [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. The rudder needs less pressure in a glide than you expect.

check.q: Your circle keeps drifting downwind of the point. Which error is it, and the fix?
check.a: Not correcting the bank for wind; steepen headed downwind and shallow headed upwind [[24:212|AFH 10-3]] [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

scenario.title: Checkride spiral on a windy afternoon
scenario.setup: You are on a commercial checkride in a four-seat high-wing trainer with a carbureted engine. The practice area is farmland at 800 feet MSL with a crossroads you can use as a reference. The wind at altitude is from the west at about 20 knots, the air is 60°F and humid, and a flight school trainer is working the same area a few thousand feet below you. The examiner asks for a steep spiral to the right, at least three turns, rolling out on a heading of north.

questions.q: What altitude do you choose, and how do you decide?
questions.a: Enough to fly at least three turns and finish no lower than 1,500 feet AGL, which here is 2,300 feet MSL (ACS CA.V.B.S2, S6). Add your expected loss per turn times three plus a margin; the AFH says to note the loss each turn [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

questions.q: Rolling steeper on the downwind side, the airspeed starts to build. What is going on and what do you do?
questions.a: A gliding turn pushes the nose down: the lift is tilted, rudder pressures feel light, and the power-off nose tends to drop [[24:84|AFH 3-23]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Add back pressure as you roll in, set the attitude on the horizon and cross-check instead of chasing the airspeed indicator [[24:85|AFH 3-24]], and stay within the ACS band of the specified speed plus or minus 10 knots (ACS CA.V.B.S6).

questions.q: The engine is carbureted and the air is humid. What do you do before and during the idle glide?
questions.a: Carburetor heat full on before closing the throttle and left on [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]], then advance the throttle for a few seconds now and then, preferably headed into the wind, holding airspeed with pitch [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. 60°F and high humidity is inside the high icing potential range [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]].

questions.q: Headed east, the airplane drifts outside your circle and you are already at 58°. What now?
questions.a: Headed east in a west wind you are downwind, where the bank must be steepest [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. You cannot go past 60° (ACS CA.V.B.S4); accept a slightly bigger circle and pick a wider radius for the next lap [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

questions.q: On the second turn the examiner points out traffic and asks you to report it. How do you handle it?
questions.a: Keep flying first. Look with smooth head movements, not sudden ones, since abrupt head movement in a prolonged turn invites the Coriolis illusion [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. Division of attention between control, traffic and ground track is part of the standard (ACS CA.V.B.S5).

questions.q: On the debrief the examiner asks why your speed control matters so much near 60°. What do you say?
questions.a: At 60° the load factor is 2 and stall speed is about 41 percent higher [[24:211|AFH 10-2]], which eats the margin above gliding speed. Let the nose drop instead and you head for a spiral dive with rising speed and G [[24:131|AFH 5-26]], and near the ground a high-speed spiral can become an unrecoverable sink [[24:103|AFH 4-17]].

skills.do: Clear the area before the maneuver.
skills.practice: Two 90° clearing turns looking left, right, above and below, plus a practice area call [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

skills.do: Choose an altitude high enough for at least three 360° turns.
skills.practice: Before each practice, say the field elevation, the 1,500 AGL floor in MSL and your start altitude; record the loss per lap [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

skills.do: Fly a steep spiral at a constant radius around a suitable ground point, never more than 60° of bank.
skills.practice: Pick the radius by your distance from the point so the downwind bank stays at or below 60° [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

skills.do: Correct for wind to keep the circle constant, with the steepest bank no more than 60°.
skills.practice: Say 'steeper' as you turn downwind and 'shallower' as you turn upwind, and watch the point stay the same distance off the wingtip [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

skills.do: Divide attention among airplane control, traffic and the ground track while staying coordinated.
skills.practice: Count laps aloud, scan for traffic each lap, and glance at the ball with every bank change [[24:85|AFH 3-24]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

skills.do: Hold the specified airspeed within 10 knots, roll out within 10° of the object or heading, and finish no lower than 1,500 feet AGL.
skills.practice: Trim for gliding speed, anticipate pitch with bank, and practice rollouts on headings into the wind and across it [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

quiz.q: What is the objective of the steep spiral?
options: To practice spin entries at altitude
To lose a lot of altitude rapidly while staying over a selected spot
To descend as fast as possible at maximum allowable airspeed
To build turn performance at full power
quiz.why: The objective is a maneuver for rapidly dissipating substantial altitude while remaining over a selected spot [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

quiz.q: How many 360° turns does the ACS require?
options: At least one
At least two
At least three
Exactly four
quiz.why: Select an altitude sufficient for a series of at least three 360° turns (ACS CA.V.B.S2) [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

quiz.q: What is the lowest altitude at which the maneuver may be completed?
options: 500 feet AGL
1,000 feet AGL
1,500 feet AGL
3,000 feet AGL
quiz.why: Complete the maneuver no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS CA.V.B.S6) [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

quiz.q: What is the maximum bank angle in the commercial steep spiral?
quiz.why: Not to exceed 60°, including at the steepest point (ACS CA.V.B.S3, S4) [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

quiz.q: Holding one bank angle, what happens to the turn radius over the ground as groundspeed increases?
options: It decreases
It increases
It stays the same
It depends only on airspeed
quiz.why: As groundspeed increases, the observed radius increases [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].

quiz.q: How does a typical emergency descent differ from a steep spiral?
options: It is flown at gliding speed with no turns
It is high drag and high airspeed, often with gear and flaps out as recommended
It always uses 60° of bank
It is flown with cruise power
quiz.why: Emergency descents are generally high drag, high airspeed procedures [[24:82|AFH 3-21]] [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]; the steep spiral is flown at gliding speed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

quiz.q: Why should you periodically advance the throttle during the spiral?
options: To keep altitude constant
To avoid excessive engine cooling, plug fouling and carburetor ice
To tighten the turn radius
To test the stall warning
quiz.why: Prolonged idle can cause excessive engine cooling, spark plug fouling or carburetor ice [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

quiz.q: Compared with a straight glide, what does a gliding turn need?
options: Less back pressure
More back pressure
No change in pitch pressure
Forward pressure
quiz.why: Three elements force the nose down in a gliding turn, so it needs more back pressure than a straight glide or a level turn [[24:84|AFH 3-23]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

quiz.q: What does the AFH say about airspeed as the bank changes in the spiral?
options: It stays constant by itself
It tends to fluctuate, so anticipate pitch corrections
It only changes with power
It should be allowed to vary up to 20 knots
quiz.why: Airspeed tends to fluctuate as bank changes; anticipate pitch corrections [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

quiz.q: Why does the AFH have simulated emergency descents made in a turn?
options: To keep load factor under 1 G
To check for traffic below and look for a landing area
To cool the engine faster
To make the descent slower
quiz.why: A turn lets you check for traffic below and look around for a possible emergency landing area [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

final_quiz.q: On your checkride spiral you hold airspeed within 8 knots, finish at 1,700 feet AGL and roll out 13° off the assigned heading. Which item fails?
options: Airspeed
Altitude
Rollout heading
None
final_quiz.why: Rollout must be within ±10°; airspeed ±10 knots and no lower than 1,500 AGL are met (ACS CA.V.B.S6).

final_quiz.q: To hold your radius headed downwind you would need 63° of bank. What is the right fix?
options: Use 63° briefly; the ACS allows it at one point
Fly a larger radius by moving farther from the reference
Add power to slow the drift
Skid with rudder to tighten the turn
final_quiz.why: Bank may not exceed 60° at the steepest point (ACS CA.V.B.S4); your distance from the reference sets the radius [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Skidding risks a cross-control spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

final_quiz.q: When is clearing the engine best done in the spiral?
options: Headed downwind, letting speed rise
Headed into the wind, adjusting pitch to hold airspeed
Only on the last turn
Only below 1,500 feet AGL
final_quiz.why: Advance the throttle for a few seconds, adjust pitch to hold airspeed, preferably headed into the wind [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

final_quiz.q: Before ground reference maneuvers, why does the AFH have you find the stall speed at the highest bank you expect?
options: To set the entry altitude
To be sure of a safety margin above the stall during the maneuver
To compute the wind correction angle
To find VNE
final_quiz.why: Determine the predicted stall speed at 50° or at the highest bank expected to assure a safety margin above the stall [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

final_quiz.q: You are in a spiral dive: nose low, steep bank, speed rising, power already at idle. What next?
options: Pull back hard while rolling level
Some forward elevator to unload, then roll wings level
Add full power and roll level
Hold the bank and pull to raise the nose
final_quiz.why: Unload with some forward elevator to about 1 G, then roll level, then gently raise the nose [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Rolling while pulling is a listed error [[24:132|AFH 5-27]].

final_quiz.q: Your engine fails at 5,000 feet AGL directly over a long, smooth field. How does the steep spiral help?
options: It lets you stay over the field and arrive at the key position at pattern altitude
It gives the fastest descent to the ground
It keeps you above 1,500 feet AGL
It restarts the engine
final_quiz.why: Use gliding maneuvers, including spirals, to arrive at the normal key position at normal pattern altitude, then fly a power-off approach [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

final_quiz.q: Why is carburetor ice especially sneaky during a long idle spiral?
options: It only forms at full power
It can build unnoticed until you add power
It raises the oil temperature
Carburetor heat makes it worse at idle
final_quiz.why: Carburetor ice is particularly dangerous at reduced power in a descent and can build unnoticed until power is added [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

final_quiz.q: What is the target at the end of the rollout?
options: Wings level at cruise power immediately
A wings-level glide with no change in airspeed, then recover to cruise
A climb at VY
A level-off at the entry altitude
final_quiz.why: Recover to a wings-level glide with no change in airspeed; recovery to cruise follows [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

final_quiz.q: Practicing alone with a non-pilot friend and no parachutes, which 14 CFR 91.307 limit could a steep spiral also run into, besides bank?
options: A 2 G load factor
A nose-down attitude of more than 30°
A descent rate of 2,000 feet per minute
A minimum altitude of 3,000 feet AGL
final_quiz.why: No intentional maneuver may exceed 60° of bank or 30° nose up or nose down relative to the horizon with a non-crew passenger and no parachutes [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]].

final_quiz.q: In a high-wing airplane, flying a left spiral from the left seat, the lowered wing hides the point. What does the AFH suggest?
options: Fly the spiral on instruments
Change the radius or altitude so the point stays visible
Lean away from the turn
Ignore the point and hold the bank
final_quiz.why: The lowered wing may block the view of the reference; change the maneuvering altitude or the radius so it is visible at all times [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].

final_quiz.q: During the downwind half of the circle, where should the nose point relative to your position over the ground?
options: Behind it, toward the outside of the turn
Ahead of it, toward the inside of the turn
Straight at the reference point
Exactly along the circle
final_quiz.why: Downwind half: heading progressively toward the inside, ahead of the position; upwind half: toward the outside, behind it [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].

final_quiz.q: Late in a long spiral you feel wings level, yet the altimeter keeps unwinding, and you want to pull back. What is happening?
options: The leans; roll the other way
Graveyard spiral; pulling back only tightens the spiral
Somatogravic illusion; push forward
Normal glide; pull back to stretch it
final_quiz.why: In a prolonged coordinated turn you can feel level while descending; pulling back tightens the spiral and increases the loss [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]] [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

final_quiz.q: In a glide, why might you need slight left rudder even though no power is set?
options: P-factor is stronger at idle
The airplane's built-in corrections for powered flight remain while the effects they cancel are gone
Carburetor heat causes yaw
The ball is always unreliable in a glide
final_quiz.why: In a glide P-factor and slipstream effects disappear but the design compensation remains, so slight left rudder is likely needed [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

takeaways: Commercial standard: at least three 360° turns, bank never past 60°, airspeed ±10 knots, rollout ±10°, finish no lower than 1,500 feet AGL.
Purpose: lose a lot of altitude while staying over one spot, the tool for getting down over a field after an engine failure.
Steeper headed downwind, shallower headed upwind; your distance from the point sets the radius.
Airspeed wanders with every bank change; lead it with pitch and trim for gliding speed.
Carburetor heat on before idle, and clear the engine now and then, preferably into the wind.
Know the stall speed at 60° and do not let the spiral become a spiral dive: unload, roll level, then raise the nose.
Clear below, keep scanning every lap, and keep your eyes outside.
cfi_notes: AFH 7-4 describes the bank for a constant ground radius as 'proportional to groundspeed' [[24:150|AFH 7-4]]. For numbers, use the PHAK radius formula with groundspeed [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]; it gives the AFH's own examples (45° at 100 knots for about 890 feet, about 33° at the 80-knot upwind point) [[24:150|AFH 7-4]].

AFH 7-2 gives 45° as a general bank limit for ground reference maneuvers [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. The steep spiral text sets the steepest bank at no more than 60° [[24:213|AFH 10-4]], and so does the ACS (ACS CA.V.B.S3, S4). Tell students coming from turns around a point which number applies to this maneuver.

The AFH recommends 30° to 45° of bank for emergency descents [[24:357|AFH 18-8]] and up to 60° for the steep spiral [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Keep the two procedures separate in the student's mind; the AFH says their airspeed and configuration usually differ [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

Have the student compute the stall speed at 60° from the POH clean stall speed and compare it with the gliding speed before the flight [[24:148|AFH 7-2]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. In some trainers the margin is small. The sources give load factor for level turns only; use those figures as the guide.
ACS S4 sets the 60° limit at the steepest point in the turn (ACS CA.V.B.S4). The AFH puts the steepest bank on downwind headings [[24:213|AFH 10-4]], so that is where to watch the limit.

The ACS asks for the 'specified airspeed' without saying who specifies it (ACS CA.V.B.S6). The AFH says gliding speed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Brief the speed with the examiner, and teach the POH best glide speed unless your syllabus says otherwise.

The AFH gives the half-bank rollout lead for steep turns [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]; the steep spiral text gives no lead rule [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. In a gliding spiral with a changing bank, teach the student to judge the lead from the actual bank and rate of turn.
During simulated engine failures and engine clearing, make it explicit who controls the throttle; the AFH notes many near accidents came from that confusion [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].
Fly right spirals as well as left ones. In a high-wing airplane the left turn hides the point under the wing from the left seat [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].
gaps: No source here gives the altitude lost per turn or the descent rate in a steep spiral; it depends on the airplane, bank and speed. Measure it on the first lap, as the AFH suggests [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
The ACS does not define the 'specified airspeed'; the gliding speed comes from the POH/AFM, and the examiner may specify another.
The sources give load factor and stall speed figures for level turns only; none gives the load factor in a descending spiral.
How often and how long to clear the engine is not quantified beyond 'periodically' and 'a few seconds' [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]; follow the POH and your CFI.
The AFH steep spiral text does not say whether flaps should be used; Figure 9-28 shows flaps retracted during the spiral down to a field [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. Use the POH and your CFI's guidance.

activities.title: Read the steep spiral picture
activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Entry: idle, gliding speed, roll in near the point
Rollout toward an object or heading

activities.title: Steeper or shallower?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Headed downwind and drifting outside the circle
Headed upwind and the circle is getting too tight

activities.title: Airspeed limits on the dial
activities.intro: Tap a marking, then the meaning that fits it.

pairs.r: VNE: beyond it structural damage could occur
VNO to VNE: smooth air only, with caution
Normal operating range, VS1 to VNO
Flap operating range, VS0 to VFE

activities.title: True or false: the engine in a long glide
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: If carburetor ice is possible, put carburetor heat full on before closing the throttle and leave it on.

cards.why: False. Heated air is less dense, so power drops, sometimes up to 15 percent [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

cards.s: Carburetor ice cannot form when the outside air is above 70°F.
cards.why: False. It is most likely below 70°F with high humidity, but can form at up to 100°F and 50 percent humidity [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]].

cards.s: A cylinder head temperature gauge gives extra information on engine cooling during the spiral.
cards.why: True [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. It shows a direct and immediate cylinder temperature change [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].

cards.s: High-speed descents can shock cool an engine.
cards.why: True. They provide excess cooling air and abrupt temperature changes [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]].

cards.s: When you advance the throttle to clear the engine, keep the same pitch and let the speed rise.
cards.why: False. Adjust the pitch to hold a constant airspeed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

activities.title: Work the spiral numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: AFH example: you want a 2,000-foot radius over the ground. Headed downwind your groundspeed is 100 knots. Using radius = speed squared / (11.26 x tan bank), what bank do you need?
Same 2,000-foot circle. Headed upwind your groundspeed is 80 knots. What bank holds the radius?
Headed downwind your groundspeed is 90 knots, and you want 55° of bank at that steepest point. Radius = speed squared / (11.26 x tan bank). What radius over the ground does that give?
Same 504-foot circle. Headed upwind your groundspeed is 60 knots. What bank do you need there?
Your POH gliding speed for the spiral is 75 knots and your clean stall speed is 52 knots. In a level 60° bank, how many knots are you above the stall speed?
items.why: Load factor at 60° = 2.0 [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Square root of 2 = 1.414. 52 x 1.414 = 73.5 knots stall speed in the bank. 75 - 73.5 = 1.5 knots of margin, almost none. Compare the two numbers before the flight [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

items.q: You lose 520 feet per turn. What is the lowest altitude AGL at which you can start three turns and finish at the ACS floor?
items.why: 3 x 520 = 1,560. 1,500 + 1,560 = 3,060 feet AGL, before any margin (ACS CA.V.B.S2, S6).

items.q: At 75 knots TAS and 60° of bank, how many seconds does one 360° take through the air? Rate = 1,091 x tan bank / TAS.

activities.title: Put the steep spiral in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Find the wind, pick a reference point and an altitude that finishes above 1,500 feet AGL
Throttle to idle, carburetor heat on, slow to gliding speed
Lower the nose and roll in as the reference point is reached
Steepen downwind and shallow upwind to hold the radius, leading airspeed with pitch
Clear the engine now and then and note the altitude lost each turn
After at least three turns, roll out on the object or heading to a wings-level glide at the same speed

activities.title: Engine out high over a field
activities.intro: You are flying a carbureted high-wing trainer at 5,500 feet AGL in cruise, on a cross-country with your CFI. The engine coughs and quits. Directly below is a long, smooth hay field. A windsock at a farm strip nearby shows a steady wind from the west.

steps.s: You are well above best glide speed. What first?
options: Lower the nose at once to keep cruise speed
Hold altitude and let the speed bleed to best glide, then pitch and trim for it
Put the flaps down to slow quickly
Start a 60° bank immediately
steps.why: Above best glide, let the airplane slow (even by climbing) to best glide speed, then lower the nose and trim for it [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

steps.s: The checklist items do not restore power. The field is right below you with lots of altitude to spare. How do you get down to it?
options: Fly away for a long straight-in so you have time
Spiral down over the field to arrive at the key position at normal pattern altitude
Dive at the field to land sooner
Fly an emergency descent at VNE
steps.why: Use gliding maneuvers, including spirals, to arrive at the normal key position at pattern altitude [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. The steep spiral exists to lose altitude over a selected spot [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

steps.s: In the spiral, the circle keeps sliding east of the field.
options: Hold the same bank all the way around
Steepen the bank headed east (downwind) and shallow it headed west (upwind)
Add rudder to skid the nose toward the field
Shallow the bank headed east
steps.why: Correct for wind by steepening on downwind headings and shallowing on upwind headings [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. Skidding a gliding turn near the ground risks a spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

steps.s: You have lost about 800 feet per turn and are now 2,200 feet above the field.
options: Keep spiraling until you are low, then roll out
Use the loss per turn to plan the last turn so you roll out at the key position
Roll out now and fly a long final
Add carburetor heat and hope for a restart
steps.why: Noting the altitude lost each turn tells you when to roll out so you are neither too high nor too low [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

steps.s: Rolling out toward the key position, you are 15 knots fast and the field edge is coming up quickly.
options: Push over to get down faster
Raise the nose back to gliding speed and use a slip or flaps to manage the extra height
Land fast and brake hard
Pull up steeply to stop the descent
steps.why: Too much speed is as dangerous as too little, and you cannot dive at a field and expect to land on it [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. Slips and flaps are ways to correct a misjudged glide [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
